sections.heading: Learning Point 1
sections.content: CONSTRUCTIONS AND TILINGS 6 6.1 Geometric Constructions Eyes Do you recall the ‘Eyes’ construction we did in Grade 6?
sections.source_evidence: CONSTRUCTIONS AND TILINGS 6 6.1 Geometric Constructions Eyes Do you recall the ‘Eyes’ construction we did in Grade 6?

sections.heading: Learning Point 2
sections.content: Of course, eyes can be drawn freehand, but we wanted to construct them so that the lower arc and upper arc of each eye look symmetrical.
sections.source_evidence: Of course, eyes can be drawn freehand, but we wanted to construct them so that the lower arc and upper arc of each eye look symmetrical.

sections.heading: Learning Point 3
sections.content: We relied on our spatial estimation to determine the two centres, A and B (see the figure), from which we drew the lower arc and upper arc respectively.
sections.source_evidence: We relied on our spatial estimation to determine the two centres, A and B (see the figure), from which we drew the lower arc and upper arc respectively.

sections.heading: Learning Point 4
sections.content: The arcs define a line XY that ‘supports’ the drawing though it is not part of the final figure.
sections.source_evidence: The arcs define a line XY that ‘supports’ the drawing though it is not part of the final figure.

sections.heading: Learning Point 5
sections.content: We can start with this supporting line and systematically find the centres A and B.
sections.source_evidence: We can start with this supporting line and systematically find the centres A and B.

sections.heading: Learning Point 6
sections.content: For the eye to be symmetrical, or for the supporting line to be the line of symmetry, the upper and lower arcs should have the same radius.
sections.source_evidence: For the eye to be symmetrical, or for the supporting line to be the line of symmetry, the upper and lower arcs should have the same radius.

sections.heading: Learning Point 7
sections.content: Since AX = AY and BX = BY, this means AX = AY = BX = BY A B X Y
sections.source_evidence: Since AX = AY and BX = BY, this means AX = AY = BX = BY A B X Y

sections.heading: Learning Point 8
sections.content: Constructions and Tilings How do we find such A and B?
sections.source_evidence: Constructions and Tilings How do we find such A and B?

sections.heading: Learning Point 9
sections.content: From X and Y, draw arcs above and below XY, with the same radii.
sections.source_evidence: From X and Y, draw arcs above and below XY, with the same radii.

sections.heading: Learning Point 10
sections.content: The two points at which the arcs meet, above and below XY, give us A and B, respectively.
sections.source_evidence: The two points at which the arcs meet, above and below XY, give us A and B, respectively.

sections.heading: Learning Point 11
sections.content: Where does AB intersect XY, and what is the angle formed between them?
sections.source_evidence: Where does AB intersect XY, and what is the angle formed between them?

sections.heading: Learning Point 12
sections.content: We observe that AB passes through the midpoint of XY, and is also perpendicular to it.
sections.source_evidence: We observe that AB passes through the midpoint of XY, and is also perpendicular to it.

sections.heading: Learning Point 13
sections.content: A division of a line, or any geometrical object, into two identical parts is called bisection.
sections.source_evidence: A division of a line, or any geometrical object, into two identical parts is called bisection.

sections.heading: Learning Point 14
sections.content: A line that bisects a given line and is perpendicular to it, is called the perpendicular bisector.
sections.source_evidence: A line that bisects a given line and is perpendicular to it, is called the perpendicular bisector.

sections.heading: Learning Point 15
sections.content: Will the line joining the two points at which the arcs meet, above and below XY, always be the perpendicular bisector of XY, i.e., when XY is of any length, and the arcs are drawn using a radius of any length?
sections.source_evidence: Will the line joining the two points at which the arcs meet, above and below XY, always be the perpendicular bisector of XY, i.e., when XY is of any length, and the arcs are drawn using a radius of any length?

sections.heading: Learning Point 16
sections.content: This can be answered through congruence.
sections.source_evidence: This can be answered through congruence.

sections.heading: Learning Point 17
sections.content: Find points A and B such that AX = AY = BX = BY.
sections.source_evidence: Find points A and B such that AX = AY = BX = BY.

sections.heading: Learning Point 18
sections.content: Let O be the point of intersection between AB and XY.
sections.source_evidence: Let O be the point of intersection between AB and XY.

sections.heading: Learning Point 19
sections.content: Which two triangles should be congruent for AB to be the perpendicular bisector of XY (that is, O is the midpoint of XY and AB is perpendicular to XY)?
sections.source_evidence: Which two triangles should be congruent for AB to be the perpendicular bisector of XY (that is, O is the midpoint of XY and AB is perpendicular to XY)?

sections.heading: Learning Point 20
sections.content: If we show that ∆AOX ≅ ΔAOY, then OX = OY, and ∠AOX = ∠AOY because they are corresponding parts of congruent triangles.
sections.source_evidence: If we show that ∆AOX ≅ ΔAOY, then OX = OY, and ∠AOX = ∠AOY because they are corresponding parts of congruent triangles.
